sections.title: STOP Recommendations
sections.html:
STOP Recommendations

The interventions below are conventional or intuitively appealing practices that are counterproductive in active tuberculosis because they relieve a host-imposed constraint on Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb). Each is paired with a mechanistic rationale and a SWAP. All are adjuncts to—never substitutes for—standard multidrug anti-TB chemotherapy.

STOP: Routine iron supplementation in active TB

The low serum iron measured in active TB is not, in most cases, true iron deficiency. It is hepcidin-driven sequestration—the hallmark of anemia of inflammation and a deliberate host defense. In a prospective study of adults with TB, hepcidin and erythroferrone were markedly elevated, erythrocyte iron utilization was high (~80%), and gastrointestinal iron absorption was negligible (<1%) before treatment; hepcidin and IL-6 fell ~70% within two weeks of effective therapy, and the anemia resolved without any iron given. {{cite:blood2021}} Supplemental iron in this setting is poorly absorbed and feeds the pathogen: Mtb deploys high-affinity siderophores (mycobactin and carboxymycobactin) to pirate iron from transferrin, lactoferrin, and ferritin, and mammalian serum is tuberculostatic precisely because it withholds iron—an effect that adding iron reverses completely. {{cite:fcimb2022}} {{cite:nienaber2023}} The clinical signal is consistent: in iron-deficient Somali nomads, those randomized to iron repletion suffered far more infectious episodes—including reactivation of latent tuberculosis—than the placebo group. {{cite:murray1978}} Across African cohorts, dietary iron overload is associated with increased TB risk and TB mortality. {{cite:fcimb2022}}

SWAP: Treat the infection—anemia of inflammation resolves with effective chemotherapy. {{cite:blood2021}} Support host iron sequestration (e.g., lactoferrin, an iron-binding glycoprotein that withholds iron from Mtb and modulates granuloma pathology). {{cite:lactoferrin2015}} Reserve iron only for documented, true iron-deficiency anemia—ideally confirmed during or after treatment when inflammation has subsided—and supplement cautiously; transfuse if anemia is severe. {{cite:nienaber2023}}

STOP / CAUTION: Hyperbaric oxygen (HBOT) and oxygenation as a strategy

Mtb is an obligate aerobe whose replication requires oxygen; the hypoxic core of the granuloma (oxygen tension ~1.6 mmHg) is a host-imposed brake that halts bacillary growth and drives it into a non-replicating, dormant state. {{cite:hypoxia2016}} {{cite:cellrep2023}} Raising tissue oxygenation therefore risks relieving exactly the constraint the host uses to contain the organism. This is the framework-consistent opposite of anaerobe-dominated conditions, where HBOT is therapeutic. This is a mechanistic caution, stated honestly: direct controlled trials of HBOT for pulmonary TB are essentially absent, and the only human data is a small uncontrolled spinal-TB case series reporting adjunctive benefit. {{cite:spinalhbot2009}} SWAP: Do not pursue hyperoxygenation as an anti-TB strategy; if HBOT is being considered for an unrelated indication in a patient with active or latent TB, weigh this mechanistic concern and prioritize effective chemotherapy.

sections.title: Validation In Progress
sections.html:
Validation In Progress

The following host-directed and repurposed adjuncts are mechanistically coherent but supported by incomplete clinical evidence. Each is listed with its mechanism, an honest evidence note, and a mechanistic-confidence flag. None replaces standard chemotherapy.

Metformin (mechanistic confidence: medium)

Mechanism: Activates AMPK, inhibits mTORC1, and restores autophagy/xenophagy, promoting maturation of Mtb-containing phagosomes and intracellular killing. {{cite:metf_mech}}

Evidence: Retrospective cohorts show metformin use in diabetics with TB is associated with lower mortality and improved 2-month culture conversion, apparently independent of glycemic control. {{cite:degner2018}} However, a randomized 8-week adjunctive trial in non-diabetic pulmonary TB (1 g/day) did not shorten time to sputum culture conversion (primary endpoint), though it was associated with faster radiographic cavity resolution and reduced inflammatory markers. {{cite:metf_rct}} Definitive RCTs are ongoing. Classify as promising but unproven for efficacy.

Statins (mechanistic confidence: medium)

Mechanism: Mtb exploits host cholesterol for entry and as a carbon source; statin-mediated cholesterol depletion enhances phagosome maturation and autophagy and may improve drug penetration into granulomas. {{cite:statin_pre}} {{cite:statin_ator}}

Evidence: Preclinical—adjunctive simvastatin shortened time to culture-negative lungs in mice. {{cite:statin_pre}} Observational—statin use is associated with reduced TB incidence in diabetic and general populations. {{cite:statin_obs}} No completed adjunctive efficacy RCT yet. Mechanistically sound, clinically unconfirmed.

Zinc + vitamin A (mechanistic confidence: low)

Mechanism: Micronutrient cofactors supporting cell-mediated immunity and epithelial integrity in often-deficient TB patients.

Evidence: Mixed and inconsistent. An early Jakarta trial reported earlier sputum conversion and radiographic resolution with zinc + vitamin A, but a subsequent trial in severely malnourished patients failed to reproduce any significant benefit on sputum conversion time. {{cite:zinc_neg}} {{cite:micronutrient_meta}} Reasonable for correcting documented deficiency; not established as an outcome-modifying adjunct.

Phenylbutyrate + vitamin D (mechanistic confidence: medium)

Mechanism: Both are inducers of the host antimicrobial peptide cathelicidin (LL-37); LL-37 drives autophagy-dependent killing of intracellular Mtb. {{cite:pba_mech}}

Evidence: A randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in Bangladesh (288 patients) of 4-phenylbutyrate and/or vitamin D3 reported beneficial effects on clinical recovery and earlier decline in intracellular Mtb growth in macrophages with raised LL-37. {{cite:pba_rct}} A single positive RCT; warrants confirmation in larger, multi-site trials.

sections.title: Research Gaps
sections.html:
Research Gaps

Several questions central to a microbiome- and host-ecology-informed approach to tuberculosis remain unresolved. We frame them as testable hypotheses.

  • Causality of the airway and gut microbiome. Does dysbiosis contribute to TB susceptibility, severity, or relapse, or is it largely a downstream consequence of long anti-TB antibiotic courses? Longitudinal, treatment-naive cohorts with pre/post-therapy sampling are needed to separate a causal microbial role from antibiotic confounding. {{cite:fcimb2022}}
  • Host iron modulation as therapy. Iron-withholding is mechanistically protective, but does deliberate iron restriction—or pharmacologic host-iron modulation (e.g., hepcidin agonists, lactoferrin, siderophore-targeting agents)—improve outcomes in randomized human trials, and what is the safe boundary of the proposed "iron benefit window"? {{cite:nienaber2023}} {{cite:blood2021}}
  • Host-directed therapy efficacy. Will repurposed agents (metformin, statins, cathelicidin inducers) shorten treatment, reduce relapse, or limit lung damage when tested in adequately powered, multi-site RCTs in both diabetic and non-diabetic populations—and in which patient subgroups? {{cite:metf_rct}} {{cite:statin_obs}}
  • Microbiome-protective strategies during therapy. Can targeted probiotics, narrower regimens, or microbiome-sparing approaches preserve commensal communities during 4–6+ month antibiotic courses without compromising cure—and does doing so reduce post-TB morbidity? {{cite:nienaber2023}}
